1930: The word blues has two main meanings — one about emotion, one about music — and they are deeply and intentionally connected.

When someone says they "have the blues," they mean they are feeling sad, low, or gloomy. It is not quite full-on depression — it is more like a soft, lingering unhappiness. You feel a bit flat, unmotivated, or melancholic. It might have a clear cause (missing someone, a hard week, bad weather) or no obvious reason at all.

Important grammar note: "The blues" almost always appears with the word the, and it is grammatically plural even though it describes one unified feeling.

  • ✓ "I have the blues."
  • ✓ "She's been feeling the blues all week."
  • ✗ "I have blues." (unusual; almost no one says this)

Common compound expressions using this sense:

  • The Monday blues (also Sunday blues): The dread or low feeling at the start of the working week, or the evening before it.
  • The baby blues: A period of emotional fragility, sadness, or tearfulness that many new mothers experience in the days after childbirth. It is a real and widely recognized emotional condition, distinct from the more serious postpartum depression.
  • The winter blues: The low mood many people experience during cold, dark winter months, largely due to reduced sunlight.

"The blues" is also one of the most important music genres ever created — and arguably the single most influential one in the history of modern Western music.

It was born among African Americans in the southern United States, especially in the Mississippi Delta region, in the late 1800s and early 1900s. It grew directly out of the hardship, grief, and longing of that community — out of lives marked by injustice and suffering. People poured all of that pain into song.

What makes blues music sound the way it does:

  • The singing is raw and emotional — it often sounds like the singer is genuinely pleading, aching, or confessing, not performing.
  • It is built on a repeating chord pattern, most famously the 12-bar blues — a simple but endlessly expressive structure that forms the foundation of countless songs across multiple genres.
  • It uses blue notes — slightly bent or flattened musical notes that give the music its signature bittersweet, melancholic quality. These notes sit "in between" the standard notes of a scale, and they are what make blues immediately recognizable to the ear.
  • The guitar is the central instrument, often played with string bends, slides, and vibrato that make it sound like a voice crying or wailing.
  • Themes in blues lyrics typically include heartbreak, loss, poverty, longing, travel, wandering, and hardship — but also resilience and survival.

The major styles of blues:

Blues is not one single sound. It has many branches:

  • Delta blues: The earliest, rawest form — acoustic, sparse, deeply emotional. Born in the Mississippi Delta. Robert Johnson is the most legendary figure of this style.
  • Chicago blues: When Delta musicians moved north to Chicago, they picked up electric guitars and played louder, more powerful music for city audiences. Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf defined this sound.
  • Texas blues: More polished, more guitar-focused, with a smoother feel. B.B. King is the towering name here.
  • Electric blues: The broad modern form of blues built on amplified instruments, which emerged in the mid-20th century and fed directly into rock music.

Some of the greatest blues artists ever: Robert Johnson, B.B. King, Muddy Waters, Son House, Bessie Smith, Howlin' Wolf, Lightnin' Hopkins, John Lee Hooker, Buddy Guy.
3. Why Both Meanings Share the Same Word

This is not a coincidence. The music was named after the feeling — because the music was the feeling, made audible.

The people who created the blues were using song to express, process, and survive the blues as an emotion. The music became a vessel for sorrow. But here is the remarkable thing about it: blues music does not just make you feel sadder. There is a quality of catharsis and aliveness in it — a release. Even a deeply mournful blues song can feel strangely energizing and liberating to listen to. This is part of why it endured and spread far beyond its origins.
4. How Blues Shaped Nearly All Modern Music

The blues did not stay in one community or one era. It spread outward and transformed into, or directly influenced, almost every major genre of popular music you can think of:

  • Rock and roll is essentially electrified blues. Chuck Berry, Little Richard, and later The Rolling Stones, Led Zeppelin, Eric Clapton, and Jimi Hendrix all built their music on blues foundations.
  • Jazz shares deep roots with the blues — blue notes, expressive improvisation, and emotional depth are central to both.
  • Soul and R&B grew organically from the blues tradition.
  • Country music has significant blues DNA, especially in its use of the guitar and its themes of loss and hardship.
  • Even hip-hop has sampled blues records and draws on the blues tradition of storytelling through struggle.

If blues suddenly vanished from musical history, nearly all of modern popular music would collapse or look completely unrecognizable.

• "She seemed distant and quiet — I think she just had the blues."
  • "The cold, gray November days always give me the winter blues."
  • "He grew up listening to Chicago blues on the radio."
  • "B.B. King was a master of the blues."
  • "That guitar solo captures everything raw and heartbroken about the blues."
  • "After the baby was born, she went through a couple of weeks of the baby blues."
  • "The Rolling Stones were heavily influenced by American blues musicians."

In a single sentence: Blues refers both to a feeling of gentle, lingering sadness (as in "I have the blues") and to a deeply emotional genre of music born from African American suffering in the American South — and both meanings are one and the same, because the music was the emotion turned into sound.
1931:
To bluff means to pretend you are in a stronger, more confident, or more capable position than you actually are, in order to trick someone into believing it — and to gain some kind of advantage as a result.

The heart of bluffing is this: you want the other person to think you hold more power, knowledge, or ability than you really do. And because they believe that, they act in a way that benefits you.
What Makes Bluffing Different from Just Lying?

This is important. Bluffing is a specific type of deception. Not all lies are bluffs. The difference is this:

  • A regular lie can be about anything.
  • A bluff is specifically about faking your own strength, confidence, capability, or position.

When you bluff, you are essentially putting on a performance — acting bold, certain, or powerful — when deep inside, you know you are not. The goal is always to make the other person back down, give in, or make a mistake because they were fooled by your false front.

Bluffing is most famously associated with the card game poker, and this example will make the meaning crystal clear.

In poker, players bet money based on the cards they hold. If you have weak cards, you are likely to lose — unless you can convince the other players that your cards are actually very strong. So you bet a large amount of money, you sit calmly, you look confident. The other players think, "This person must have excellent cards — I should quit before I lose more money." They fold (quit the round), and you win — even though your cards were terrible all along.

You never had real strength. You performed strength. That performance was the bluff.

Bluffing is not limited to card games. People bluff all the time in real life:

At work: Imagine someone in a job interview who doesn't fully know how to use a certain software. But instead of admitting it, they say confidently, "Yes, I have experience with that." They are bluffing — pretending to have a skill they don't quite have, hoping they won't be tested on it right away.

In an argument or negotiation: A person selling a car might say, "I already have two other buyers interested in this car — you'd better decide quickly." Maybe that's true, maybe it isn't. If they said it just to pressure you into deciding, that was a bluff — faking that they have more options and power than they actually do.

Between countries: A government might threaten serious consequences against another country, even if it has no real intention or ability to follow through. If the other country backs down because of that threat, the bluff worked.

In everyday conversation: If a teacher asks a question and you don't know the answer, but you give a vague, confident-sounding response hoping they won't probe further — you're bluffing your way through it.

This is a very common phrase. It means to get through a situation you weren't genuinely prepared for, by pretending to know more or be more capable than you are.

"He had never actually managed a team before, but he bluffed his way through the first few months."

It implies that you survived or succeeded — not because of real ability — but because you acted like you had it together.

This is one of the most important related phrases you'll encounter.

To call someone's bluff means to challenge their bluff directly, forcing them to prove that what they're claiming is actually true — knowing (or suspecting) that they can't.

Going back to poker: if you suspect your opponent doesn't actually have strong cards despite their confident betting, you don't quit. Instead, you match their bet and say, "Show me your cards." You called their bluff. Now they have to reveal the truth — that they were pretending.

In real life: If a coworker keeps threatening to quit every time they don't get their way, but you (and everyone else) suspect they never actually will, your manager might one day say, "Alright, if that's how you feel, we accept your resignation." That's calling the bluff — essentially saying, "Okay, prove it." If the person was indeed bluffing, they'll back down and suddenly find a reason to stay.

Bluffing only works if the other person doesn't see through it. If they do, your bluff is exposed and you've lost your advantage — often along with your credibility. This is why bluffing carries a risk. A good bluff requires you to be convincing and also to know your audience — if they can see through you, bluffing backfires badly.

To bluff is to deliberately project false confidence, strength, or ability in order to deceive others into acting in your favour — and the whole game depends on whether they believe your performance or see right through it.
1932: A blunder is a mistake — but not just any mistake. It is a mistake that is serious, embarrassing, and avoidable, usually caused by carelessness, poor judgment, or a shocking lack of thought. It is the kind of mistake that makes people think, "How could someone have gotten that so wrong?"
What Makes a Blunder a Blunder?

Not every mistake is a blunder. A blunder has a very specific character. Think of it as having three key qualities working together:

1. It is significant.
A blunder is not a tiny slip. Spelling a word wrong in a casual text message is not a blunder. But a doctor prescribing the completely wrong medication to a patient? That is a blunder. A blunder carries real weight — it has consequences, causes problems, or causes embarrassment.

2. It was avoidable.
This is the heart of what a blunder is. A blunder happens not because a situation was genuinely difficult or impossible to navigate, but because someone was not careful enough, did not think clearly, or exercised poor judgment. It is a mistake that a reasonable amount of care or thought would have prevented. This is exactly why blunders feel so frustrating — to the person who made it and to the people around them.

3. It reflects badly on the person who made it.
Because a blunder is avoidable, it carries a sense of foolishness or clumsiness attached to it. When someone commits a blunder, others (and often the person themselves) feel that they should have known better. There is almost always an element of embarrassment involved.

If you imagine a scale of mistakes going from small to catastrophic, a blunder sits firmly in the middle-to-serious range.

  • It is more serious than a slip (a tiny, almost meaningless error, like saying the wrong word by accident mid-sentence).
  • It is more serious than a minor mistake (like forgetting to add a point in an email).
  • It is roughly similar to, or slightly heavier than, an error in judgment.
  • It is not necessarily the most catastrophic thing that can happen, but it is significant enough to cause real damage — to a plan, a reputation, a relationship, a game, or a situation.

In short: a blunder is bad enough that people notice it, talk about it, and remember it.

The word "blunder" carries a certain emotional weight. When you hear it, it almost always implies:

  • Embarrassment — the person who made it feels (or should feel) embarrassed.
  • Frustration — others are often frustrated because it was so preventable.
  • A sense of "how could this happen?" — there is almost always an air of disbelief around a blunder.

This emotional tone is part of what separates "blunder" from a plain, neutral word like "error." An error is cold and technical. A blunder is warm with embarrassment and foolishness.

Blunders can happen in virtually any area of life. Here are some clear, real-world examples across different areas:

In politics:
A government minister accidentally reveals secret information during a press conference. That is a political blunder — serious, embarrassing, and entirely avoidable.

In sports (especially chess):
The word "blunder" is used very heavily in chess. If a player moves a piece in a way that carelessly gives away their queen — the most powerful piece on the board — for no good reason, that is called a blunder. It is a move so bad that it shocks people watching.

In business:
A company launches a product with a name that, in another language, means something offensive. Nobody checked. Sales collapse in that market. That is a blunder — a costly, embarrassing, and completely avoidable mistake.

In everyday social life:
You are at a dinner party. You ask a woman when her baby is due — and she is not pregnant. That is a social blunder. It is awkward, embarrassing, and something you could have avoided by simply not assuming.

In medicine or science:
A researcher accidentally contaminates their own experiment because they forgot to follow a basic safety step. The entire experiment is ruined. That is a blunder in a professional context.

Understanding a word deeply means knowing how it is different from words that seem similar.

Mistake — This is the most general word. Every blunder is a mistake, but not every mistake is a blunder. A mistake can be small, understandable, or even easy to make. A blunder carries the extra weight of being serious, embarrassing, and avoidable.

Error — "Error" is neutral and formal. It describes a deviation from what is correct. It does not carry emotional weight. Scientists make errors in calculations. A blunder, by contrast, implies carelessness or poor judgment, not just a miscalculation.

Gaffe — A gaffe is specifically a social blunder — an embarrassing thing someone says or does in a social or public situation. All gaffes are blunders, but not all blunders are gaffes (a chess blunder, for example, is not a gaffe).

Slip — A slip is a small, accidental, often momentary mistake — like saying the wrong name or pressing the wrong button. It does not carry the weight or consequence of a blunder.

Oversight — An oversight is when something is forgotten or missed, often unintentionally. It is milder and less loaded than a blunder, and does not necessarily imply poor judgment — just that something was not noticed.
Common Ways "Blunder" Is Used as a Noun

Here are natural, everyday expressions you will encounter:

  • "That was a costly blunder." — The mistake had serious financial or practical consequences.
  • "The manager made a terrible blunder." — He exercised very poor judgment.
  • "It was a blunder of the highest order." — It was an exceptionally bad mistake.
  • "The team's blunder in the final minutes cost them the game." — A mistake at a crucial moment led to a bad outcome.
  • "Her blunder went viral on social media." — Her embarrassing mistake became very public.
  • "He committed a serious diplomatic blunder." — He made an embarrassing mistake in a formal, international setting.

To summarize everything into one clean idea:

A blunder is a serious, embarrassing, and avoidable mistake, made due to carelessness, poor judgment, or a failure to think carefully. It is bad enough to cause real harm or embarrassment, and it carries a sense of "this really should not have happened."

If you remember just one thing: a blunder is not a hard mistake that anyone could have made — it is the kind of mistake that makes people shake their heads and think, "They really should have known better."
1933:
To blunder means to make a serious mistake — usually because of carelessness, poor judgment, or not thinking carefully enough before acting.

But here is the important thing: a blunder is not just any mistake. It carries a specific feeling with it — the sense that the mistake was avoidable. The person who blundered should have known better, or should have been more careful. That is what gives the word its weight.

"The general blundered by sending his soldiers into a trap that he should have seen coming."

The verb "blunder" has two related but distinct uses:

① To make a careless or foolish mistake
This is the most common and important meaning. When someone blunders, they do something wrong in a way that is noticeable, often embarrassing, and usually the result of not paying attention or not thinking things through.

"The doctor blundered when he gave the patient the wrong medication."
"The company blundered by ignoring its customers' complaints for too long."

② To move in a clumsy, uncontrolled way — as if lost or blind
This is the more physical meaning. When someone blunders through or around a space, they stumble through it awkwardly, without direction or clear sight.

"He blundered through the dark room, knocking things off the shelves."
"She blundered around the unfamiliar kitchen, unable to find anything."

Notice how both meanings share the same feeling — a lack of control, a lack of careful thought. That is the soul of this word.
What Makes a Blunder Different from a Regular Mistake

This is where many learners stop short, so let us be precise.

IdeaWhat it really means

Think of mistakes on a scale. At one end, you have a slip — a tiny, almost excusable error, like accidentally typing the wrong letter. In the middle, you have a general mistake or error — something went wrong, but it could happen to anyone. At the more serious end, you have a blunder — a mistake that is hard to excuse, because it came from clear carelessness or poor judgment.

A blunder also often carries public embarrassment. When someone blunders, other people tend to notice. It is not a quiet, private error. It is the kind of mistake that makes people shake their heads or wince.

One more thing: a blunder usually has real consequences. It is not harmless. A chess player who blunders loses an important piece. A politician who blunders loses public trust. A surgeon who blunders puts a life at risk.

Here are natural, real-life examples so you can see how the word lives in actual use:

  • "The negotiator blundered by revealing too much information too soon."
  • "I completely blundered — I called my teacher by the wrong name in front of the whole class."
  • "The government blundered badly in its handling of the crisis."
  • "Tired and disoriented, she blundered down the wrong corridor."
  • "He blundered through his speech, forgetting entire sections he had rehearsed."

"Blunder" is often used with specific prepositions that change the picture slightly:

Blunder into — to stumble carelessly into a situation without realizing what you are getting into.

"He blundered into a private conversation and made everything awkward."

Blunder through — to get through something in a clumsy, unimpressive way, without real skill or clarity.

"She blundered through the interview, giving vague and confused answers."

Blunder around — to move or act without direction, looking lost or confused.

"The new employee blundered around for weeks before finally understanding his role."

Blunder badly / blunder seriously — these intensifiers are very natural with this verb, emphasizing the gravity of the mistake.

"The team blundered badly in the final minutes of the match."

To truly own a word, you need to know how it sits among its neighbors.

To err is simply to make a mistake — it is neutral and formal. It carries no judgment about how or why the mistake happened.

"To err is human." — no blame, no embarrassment implied.

To slip up is to make a small, usually minor mistake. It is forgivable and often trivial.

"I slipped up and forgot to send the email."

To bungle means to carry out a task badly — to mess it up through incompetence or clumsiness. It focuses on the doing of something poorly, not just a single error.

"They bungled the entire rescue operation."

To fumble suggests a physical or mental awkwardness — reaching for something and missing, or struggling to handle a situation smoothly.

"He fumbled with the keys in the dark."

To blunder, by contrast, always implies that the mistake was bigger, more avoidable, and more consequential than a slip or fumble. It is the word you reach for when someone does something that makes you think, "How could they not have seen that coming?"
When to Use It and When NOT to Use It

Use "blunder" when:

  • The mistake was careless and avoidable
  • The mistake had noticeable, real consequences
  • There is a sense that the person should have known better
  • You want to express that the error reflects poor judgment

Do not use "blunder" when:

  • The mistake was tiny and harmless (use slip or slip up)
  • The person genuinely had no way of knowing better — an honest, understandable mistake (use err or mistake)
  • The error required specialist knowledge to avoid — it would be unfair to call a layperson's technical misstep a "blunder"

Finally, pay attention to the tone of "blunder." It is a word with weight. When you say someone blundered, you are not being completely neutral — there is a mild judgment inside the word. You are saying, in effect: "This mistake was significant, it was careless, and it mattered."

It can be used critically, but also humorously or self-deprecatingly, especially when someone uses it about themselves.

"I absolutely blundered there — I should have read the instructions first."

Said with a laugh, it becomes a way of owning a mistake openly and honestly.

In short: to blunder is to make a serious, careless, avoidable mistake — or to move through something in a clumsy, directionless way. It is a word that holds accountability, consequence, and often a quiet embarrassment, all at once.
1934: "Blunt" has two distinct meanings — one about physical objects, the other about people and how they communicate. Both meanings share the same underlying idea: the absence of sharpness.

When something physical is described as blunt, it means its edge or tip is dull — worn down or never sharp to begin with. It cannot cut, pierce, or slice cleanly the way a sharp object can.

A blunt knife struggles to cut through a tomato. Instead of slicing cleanly, it tears. A blunt pencil leaves thick, fuzzy lines because its tip is rounded and worn. A blunt needle is painful and difficult to use because it pushes through instead of piercing precisely.

The opposite of blunt, in this sense, is sharp.

You'll commonly see it paired with words like knife, scissors, blade, needle, or tool. One special combination worth knowing is "blunt force" or "blunt force trauma" — terms used in medicine and law to describe an injury caused by a non-sharp object (like a rock, bat, or fist) that hits and crushes rather than cuts.
Meaning 2: Direct and Plain in Speech (people and communication)

This is the meaning you'll encounter far more often in everyday life. When a person, remark, or style of communication is blunt, it means it is direct, plain, and honest — delivered without softening the message, without diplomatic padding, and without "beating around the bush."

A blunt person says exactly what they mean. They don't sugarcoat. They don't give vague hints. They don't choose careful, gentle words to make a hard truth sound easier than it is. They just say it — plainly and directly.

Consider this contrast. A non-blunt person might say: "I think there are perhaps a few areas where this project might benefit from a little more work." A blunt person says the same thing as: "This project isn't ready. It needs a lot of work." Both people are saying the exact same thing. Only one of them is being blunt.

Another example: a blunt doctor might tell a patient directly, "You need to lose weight or your health will get worse." A less blunt doctor might ease into the very same truth over several soft, careful sentences. The message is identical; the delivery is completely different.

The phrase "to be blunt" or "to put it bluntly" is extremely common in English. When someone says it, they are signaling: I'm about to say something honest and direct — brace yourself. For example: "To be blunt, I don't think you're ready for this role."

The opposite of blunt, in this sense, is tactful, diplomatic, or roundabout.
The Connection Between the Two Meanings

The link is metaphorical and quite elegant. A sharp knife cuts through things with precision and ease. In the same way, a sharp communicator chooses carefully aimed, precise words. A blunt object doesn't cut — it just hits directly, without finesse. A blunt person communicates the same way — they hit you with the plain truth, without carefully maneuvering around it.
Is Being Blunt Positive or Negative?

This is a nuance that trips up many learners, and the honest answer is: it depends.

Bluntness can be a positive quality. People often respect it because it signals honesty. A blunt person won't deceive you, won't hide hard truths behind flattery, and won't waste your time with vague language. In close friendships, people sometimes say things like: "I love how blunt she is with me — I always know where I stand." In high-stakes situations — medical appointments, legal advice, safety discussions — bluntness is often preferred because clarity matters more than comfort. The phrase "refreshingly blunt" captures this positive shade perfectly: the directness comes as a welcome relief.

Bluntness can also be a negative quality. When someone delivers a hard truth without any warmth or awareness of the other person's feelings, bluntness can feel cold, harsh, or rude. "He was so blunt about it — he didn't even stop to see how I was feeling." Here, the person isn't just being honest — they're being insensitive.

The key thing to understand is that bluntness describes how something is said — directly, without softening — not the intention behind it. A blunt person might be warm-hearted and kind but simply not careful with their words. Or they might genuinely not care about your feelings. The tone, the relationship, and the situation tell you which it is.

"To be blunt" / "To put it bluntly" — used to introduce a frank statement: "To put it bluntly, this plan won't work."

"Blunt honesty" — honesty delivered without softening or cushioning.

"A blunt remark" — a comment that is direct and possibly harsh.

"Blunt criticism" — criticism given plainly and directly, without diplomatic padding.

"Blunt force trauma" — a medical and legal term for injury caused by a non-sharp object hitting the body.

Blunt (adjective) means either not sharp — describing a physical edge or point that is dull (a blunt knife, a blunt pencil) — or direct and plain in speech, describing a person or remark that delivers an honest message without softening or diplomacy (a blunt comment, a blunt person, "to be blunt"). Both meanings point to the same core idea: something that doesn't cut with precision or careful finesse, but hits plainly and directly.
1935:
To blunt something means to reduce its sharpness, strength, or power — to make something that was once forceful, intense, or effective become weaker and less powerful.

Think of it this way: imagine a freshly sharpened kitchen knife. It cuts cleanly and easily. Now imagine using that knife every day for months without sharpening it. The edge gradually wears down. The knife becomes less effective at cutting. That process — the gradual weakening of something sharp and powerful — is exactly what "blunt" means as a verb.

In its most physical, concrete sense, to blunt something means to make a sharp edge or point less sharp.

"Cutting through thick rope will blunt the scissors."
"Years of use had blunted the old axe."

Here, the sharpness is physical — a blade, a tip, an edge.

This is where the word truly lives, and where you'll encounter it most often. In everyday language, "blunt" is used far more often in a non-physical sense — to describe how the force, impact, or intensity of something abstract is reduced or weakened.

Anything that was once strong, sharp, or powerful can be "blunted":

Pain can be blunted:

"The medication blunted the pain, making it bearable."

The pain didn't disappear completely — it just became less sharp and intense.

Emotions can be blunted:

"Years of hardship had blunted his excitement about life."

He still felt things, but the sharpness of feeling — the joy, the passion — had worn down over time.

Criticism or opposition can be blunted:

"The politician's quick apology blunted the public's anger."

The anger still existed, but its force and edge were reduced.

An effect or impact can be blunted:

"The heavy rain blunted the effectiveness of the army's attack."

The attack still happened, but it was less powerful than it could have been.

Appetite or desire can be blunted:

"Eating a large lunch blunted his appetite for dinner."

The senses can be blunted:

"Loud noise over many years can blunt a person's sense of hearing."
The Most Important Nuance: Blunting Is Not Eliminating

This is crucial. When something is blunted, it is not destroyed or removed — it is weakened. There is still pain, still emotion, still impact — but less of it. The "sharpness" is taken away, not the thing itself.

This is what makes "blunt" a precise and useful word. It sits in between "nothing changed" and "it was completely wiped out." It describes a middle ground where something is reduced but not erased.

Compare:

  • "The drug eliminated the pain." → Pain is gone completely.
  • "The drug blunted the pain." → Pain is still there, but softer, duller, less intense.

The second sentence is a more honest and accurate thing to say in many real-life situations, which is why "blunted" is so commonly used in medical, emotional, and social contexts.

Broadly, you can blunt anything that has the quality of sharpness, force, or intensity — whether literal or figurative. In practice, you'll often see it paired with things like:

pain, impact, effect, force, enthusiasm, ambition, appetite, emotion, criticism, anger, senses, the edge of something, and competition.

"Blunt" is a transitive verb, meaning it always acts on something — it needs an object. You blunt something. You don't just "blunt" on its own.

It works in all the usual tenses:

  • "The injury blunts his speed." (present)
  • "The news blunted our excitement." (past)
  • "The cold weather is blunting the effect of the medicine." (continuous)

It is also very commonly used in the passive voice — where something gets blunted by a force acting on it:

  • "His ambition was blunted by repeated failure."
  • "The blade gets blunted quickly if you use it carelessly."
  • "Her passion for the job had been blunted by years of poor management."

In the passive form, the focus shifts from who or what is doing the blunting to what is being affected — which is often more natural and expressive.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

One more thing worth knowing: "blunt" often carries a slightly sad or unfortunate tone when used figuratively. When someone's enthusiasm is blunted, or their hope is blunted, it suggests that something has been lost — that life, time, suffering, or circumstances have worn something down that was once bright and sharp. It captures a kind of quiet diminishing that single words like "reduce" or "weaken" don't fully express.

This emotional undertone is part of what makes "blunt" such a powerful and expressive word in writing and speech.

To blunt = to take the sharpness, force, or intensity out of something — physically or figuratively — without necessarily eliminating it entirely.

It is the verb for describing the moment when something strong, sharp, or powerful begins to lose its edge.
1936:
Bluntness is the quality of saying exactly what you think or feel — directly, plainly, and without softening your words to protect someone's feelings.

When a person has bluntness, they don't dress up their opinions in polite language. They say the thing as it is. No sugar-coating. No careful hedging. No "well, in a way, perhaps, if I might say so…" — just the bare truth, stated plainly.

Imagine your friend shows you a business plan they worked on for months. They're excited and proud of it.

A person without bluntness might say: "It's interesting! There are some areas that could maybe use a little more thought, but overall you've clearly put in real effort."

A person with bluntness would say: "This won't work. The pricing is wrong, the target audience is too vague, and three of your competitors already do this better."

Same truth. Completely different delivery. The second person is showing bluntness — they said the hard thing directly, without wrapping it in comfortable words.

Bluntness is not just about what you say. It's about how little effort you make to cushion it.

It carries two ideas at once:

1. Honesty and directness. The blunt person isn't lying or hiding. They're being transparent. You always know where you stand with them. There's no guessing what they really think.

2. A lack of tact. Tact is the social skill of being honest while also being careful about how your words land. Bluntness is largely the absence of that carefulness. The blunt person is focused on the truth of the message, not on managing how it feels to receive it.
The Double Nature of Bluntness: Strength or Flaw?

This is the most important thing to understand about bluntness — it is neither purely good nor purely bad. It depends entirely on the situation and the degree.

When bluntness is a strength:

  • In a workplace where people waste time dancing around problems, bluntness cuts through the noise and gets things done.
  • When someone needs honest feedback to improve — a writer, a job candidate, a student — bluntness gives them real, usable information instead of empty reassurance.
  • In a crisis, bluntness is valuable. You don't need gentle phrasing when something is on fire. You need clear, direct instructions.
  • It builds trust over time. People who know a blunt person learn that when they say something good, they mean it — it isn't just flattery.

When bluntness is a flaw:

  • When someone is going through emotional pain and needs comfort, not an accurate assessment of their situation, bluntness can be cruel.
  • When the blunt person doesn't pick up on social context — a funeral, a fragile friendship, a sensitive moment — their directness becomes hurtfulness.
  • Bluntness without empathy can feel like carelessness, as if the speaker doesn't care about your feelings at all.
  • It can damage relationships, especially with people who feel strongly about how things are said, not just what is said.

The difference between admirable bluntness and hurtful bluntness often comes down to intent and compassion. Is the person being direct because they genuinely want to help, or because they can't be bothered to consider your feelings?

Bluntness isn't all-or-nothing. It exists on a scale.

At the mild end, a blunt person might skip small talk and get straight to the point in a conversation. They might give you feedback without adding five compliments first.

At the stronger end, they might tell you something genuinely painful without pausing to check whether you're ready to hear it, or without framing it in a way that acknowledges your feelings at all.

At the extreme end, bluntness can cross into rudeness — where the directness becomes harsh, cold, or even contemptuous.

Understanding how bluntness relates to nearby words will sharpen your understanding considerably.

Directness is the closest relative. To be direct is to say things plainly and without unnecessary detours. Directness is almost always seen as a positive quality. Bluntness is like directness, but with a sharper edge — it carries the extra suggestion that feelings may not be carefully managed.

Frankness means being open and honest, willing to say true things even when they're uncomfortable. It's similar to bluntness but a bit warmer. A frank person is honest but usually still considerate. Bluntness implies even less softening than frankness.

Tactlessness is when someone says something true (or even just their opinion) without any awareness of how it will affect the other person. Tactlessness is bluntness at its most socially clumsy. It's bluntness without the self-awareness that bluntness can sometimes have.

Rudeness is when words are unkind, disrespectful, or offensive — sometimes intentionally so. Bluntness is not rudeness, though a blunt person can sound rude to people who are accustomed to softened speech. The difference is that bluntness is about directness, while rudeness is about disrespect.

Honesty is simply the quality of being truthful. Bluntness is one particular style of delivering honesty — the unvarnished, unpadded kind.

• "Her bluntness was refreshing — she told me exactly what was wrong with my resume instead of vague encouragement."
  • "His bluntness, though sometimes uncomfortable, was the reason everyone trusted his opinion."
  • "She meant no harm, but her bluntness hurt him more than she realized."
  • "In negotiations, his bluntness was seen as aggression by people who weren't used to it."
  • "There's a difference between bluntness and cruelty — one comes from honesty, the other from indifference."
The Feeling of Being on the Receiving End

When someone is blunt with you, the experience can feel startling at first — especially if you're used to people softening their words. You might feel a sting, a jolt of surprise, or even a flash of hurt. But very often, once the initial reaction passes, you realize you actually got something valuable: a clear, honest answer that you can work with.

Over time, many people come to genuinely appreciate bluntness in the people around them, because there is a special kind of relief in knowing that what someone says to you is exactly what they mean — no performance, no hidden meaning, no polite lies.

Bluntness is the quality of speaking directly and honestly without softening your words — a trait that can be a sign of integrity and courage when handled with care, and a source of unnecessary hurt when it ignores the feelings of others entirely.
1937: To blur means to make something unclear, or to become unclear — so unclear that the edges, details, or differences are hard to see, think about, or understand. Think of it as the opposite of "sharpening." When you sharpen something, you make it clearer and more defined. When you blur something, you do the opposite — you make it fuzzy, hazy, or mixed up.

This is important: "blur" works in two directions, and you need to understand both.

1. You blur something (you cause it).
Someone or something actively causes the blurring.

"Crying blurred her vision."
"He accidentally blurred the ink by touching it before it dried."

2. Something blurs (it happens on its own).
No one is directly causing it — it just happens.

"The trees blurred as the train picked up speed."
"After so many years, her memories began to blur."

Both are correct uses. The word is flexible that way.
The Three Main Ways "Blur" Is Used

1. Visual Blurring — Things You Can See Become Unclear

This is the most common, everyday use. When something blurs visually, you can no longer see it clearly. Its edges, shape, or details become fuzzy and hard to make out.

This happens with your eyes:

"Her eyes filled with tears, and everything blurred in front of her."
"If you stare at a bright screen for too long, the text starts to blur."

This happens with photos, videos, and cameras:

"The photographer blurred the background so that only the subject was sharp."
"The speeding car blurred on the security footage."

This happens with ink, paint, or writing:

"The rain blurred the ink on the letter."
"Be careful not to smudge the page — it will blur your handwriting."

The key idea here: a thing that was once sharp and clear has lost its sharpness.

2. Mental Blurring — Thoughts, Memories, or Perception Become Unclear

Your mind can also "blur" things. When a memory, a thought, or your sense of time becomes hazy and hard to recall or understand, we use "blur."

"After the accident, the days blurred together — she couldn't tell Tuesday from Thursday."
"Exhaustion blurred his thinking, and he couldn't focus on anything."
"The details of that night have blurred over time. I can hardly remember what happened."

Notice the phrase "blurred together" in the first example. This is very natural in English. It means things that were once separate have merged into one fuzzy, indistinct whole — like when a very busy or painful week feels like one long, unclear stretch of time.

3. Conceptual Blurring — The Difference Between Two Things Becomes Unclear

This is the most abstract and perhaps the most intellectually rich use of "blur." Here, the word is used to describe a situation where a clear line or distinction between two separate ideas, roles, or categories starts to fade away, making it hard to say where one ends and the other begins.

This is most commonly used in the phrase "blur the line(s)" or "blur the distinction/boundary."

"Working from home has blurred the line between professional life and personal life."

In this sentence, professional life and personal life used to be clearly separated — you were at work, or you were at home. Now the boundary is fuzzy. They have merged. It is hard to tell one from the other.

More examples:

"Modern technology has blurred the line between human intelligence and artificial intelligence."
"His films blur the boundary between documentary and fiction."
"This new policy blurs the distinction between citizens and non-citizens."

This use of "blur" is extremely common in news articles, academic writing, and thoughtful conversation. Whenever boundaries that were once clear start to dissolve, "blur" is the right word.

"Blur" is not the same as "erase" or "destroy." When something is erased, it is completely gone. When something blurs, it still exists — but it is no longer clear or sharp. A blurred image is still an image. A blurred memory is still a memory. A blurred line is still a line of some kind — it is just no longer precise.

This is the crucial difference: blur is about losing clarity, not losing existence.
How the Word Behaves in a Sentence

"Blur" can be followed by various objects. Here are the most common patterns:

Blur + vision / sight / eyes

"The smoke blurred his vision."

Blur + the line(s) / boundary / distinction / difference

"Social media has blurred the line between public and private."

Blur + memories / thoughts / mind

"Stress had blurred her memories of the event."

Blur + together

"All the faces blurred together in the crowd."

Something blurs (no object)

"The road ahead blurred in the heat."

Whenever you want to use or understand "blur" as a verb, ask yourself this question: "Is something losing its sharpness, clarity, or clear boundaries?" If yes, "blur" is almost certainly the right word — whether you are talking about eyesight, a photograph, a memory, or an idea.
1938:
A blurb is a short piece of writing that describes something — usually a book, a film, a product, or a person — in a way that makes it sound appealing and worth your attention. It is almost always promotional, meaning its job is to attract, impress, or persuade.

The key qualities of a blurb are that it is brief, positive in tone, and written with a purpose: to make you interested in something.
The most classic example: the book blurb

Pick up any novel and flip it over. On the back cover, you will usually find a short paragraph — maybe two — that tells you what the book is about and makes it sound exciting. That is a blurb. It does not tell you the whole story. It does not give an honest review with weaknesses. It simply gives you just enough to make you curious and want to read the book.

For example, a blurb for a thriller might say something like: "When a detective receives an anonymous letter, she is pulled into a conspiracy that goes all the way to the top. Time is running out. And she might be next." Notice how it is short, dramatic, and designed to hook you — that is the job of a blurb.

There is a second type of blurb you will often see on books, and it works differently. Here, a famous author, a celebrity, or a respected expert writes a short quote praising the book. Something like: "A masterpiece. I couldn't put it down." — placed on the cover with their name underneath.

This is also called a blurb. In this case, the blurb is not a description of the book — it is a public recommendation. The idea is that if someone you admire praises a book, you are more likely to trust it and buy it. Authors and publishers actively seek these kinds of blurbs from well-known people before a book is published.

The word has spread well beyond books in modern usage. You will encounter it in many other situations:

  • Films and TV shows — The short description you see on a streaming platform before you click on a show? That is a blurb.
  • Products — A short, punchy description on a product page or a flyer that highlights the best features.
  • Professional bios — When a speaker is introduced at a conference, or when someone's short biography appears on a website or in a programme, that is often called a speaker blurb or a bio blurb. It gives just enough information about the person to establish their credibility and make them sound impressive.
  • Job applications and websites — People sometimes write a blurb about themselves: a short, confident paragraph describing who they are and what they do.
What makes something a blurb and not something else?

It helps to understand how a blurb is different from similar things:

Blurb vs. synopsis: A synopsis is a neutral, factual summary of what happens in a story — it tells you the plot, events, characters, sometimes the ending. A blurb may borrow from a synopsis, but its goal is to sell, not just to inform. A blurb is written with excitement and positive spin. A synopsis is written to inform.

Blurb vs. review: A review is a detailed critical analysis — it evaluates strengths and weaknesses and gives an honest, balanced opinion. A blurb is short and almost always glowing. You will rarely see a blurb that says anything negative.

Blurb vs. tagline: A tagline is a single, punchy line — like "Just do it" or "In space, no one can hear you scream." A blurb is a bit longer — at least a few sentences, sometimes a short paragraph.

The simplest way to remember the distinction: if it is short, promotional, and designed to make something look good, it is a blurb.

Blurbs tend to use enthusiastic language — words like gripping, brilliant, unmissable, breathtaking, essential. They use short punchy sentences. They create intrigue or urgency. They talk up the best qualities and skip the flaws. This is why blurbs can sometimes feel a little over-the-top or exaggerated — because they are, by nature, not objective. Their purpose is to attract, not to give a balanced judgement.
How it is used in sentences

• "The blurb on the back of the book made it sound like a thriller, but it turned out to be quite slow."
  • "Can you write a short blurb for our new product launch?"
  • "The author asked three famous writers to write blurbs for the novel before it was published."
  • "Her conference blurb described her as a leading voice in climate policy."
  • "I need to write a personal blurb for my profile on the company website."
A blurb is a short, positive, promotional piece of writing that describes a book, film, product, or person in a way designed to attract interest or admiration.
1939:
Blurred describes something that is not clear, not sharp, or not well-defined — something whose edges, details, or divisions are difficult to make out.

The best way to grasp it is through contrast. Think of a clear photograph versus a blurred one. In a clear photo, every detail is sharp — you can see the exact outline of every object, fine textures, precise edges. In a blurred photo, everything looks smudgy or fuzzy. Outlines become soft, details disappear, and things that should be separate seem to melt into one another. That experience — of something losing its sharpness and becoming hard to distinguish — is the heart of what "blurred" means.

In its most literal use, blurred describes things that the eye cannot see clearly. Blurred vision means your eyes can't focus properly, so everything around you appears fuzzy and indistinct — the way things look when you first wake up, or when someone who needs glasses looks at a sign. A blurred photograph is one that came out of focus, perhaps because the camera shook or the subject was moving too fast. A blurred figure in the distance is one you can't quite make out — you can see something is there, but not clearly enough to identify it.

The defining quality in the visual sense is that edges and details are not sharp. Things that should appear distinct look like they're softening and bleeding into each other.
In the abstract sense — blurred lines and boundaries

This is where "blurred" becomes especially powerful and widely used. It describes situations in life, thought, or society where two things that are supposed to be clearly separate have become mixed, overlapping, and hard to tell apart.

Imagine two countries with a sharp, clear border between them. Now imagine that in real life, people on both sides speak the same language, follow the same customs, and nobody quite agrees where one country ends and the other begins. That real-world line has become blurred.

This kind of usage appears everywhere in English. "Working from home has blurred the boundaries between professional and personal life" — because when your office is your living room, the clear separation between work time and personal time dissolves into something messy and undefined. "The line between fact and fiction has become blurred in modern media" — because it's increasingly hard to tell real news from invented stories. "The blurred distinction between art and advertising" — because some commercials are made with so much creativity and beauty that they feel indistinguishable from art.

In every case, the pattern is the same: two things that were clearly separate have lost the sharp division between them, and it has become difficult — sometimes impossible — to tell where one ends and the other begins.
In the context of memory and perception

"Blurred" also describes memories and mental experiences that are vague and imprecise. "My memories of that summer are blurred" means you can't recall the details with clarity — you know things happened, but the specifics are hazy and uncertain, much like a photograph that didn't come out sharp. "A blurred sense of reality" describes a state of mind where a person's grasp of what is real and what isn't lacks precision — things feel indistinct and uncertain in the mind.

No matter how it's used, blurred always conveys a sense of lost definition. Something that was — or should be — clearly defined has lost that quality. It has become fuzzy, hazy, or indistinct. And this almost always makes things harder to work with: a blurred photo is harder to interpret, a blurred boundary is harder to respect or enforce, a blurred memory is harder to rely on and trust.

So when you see the word "blurred," ask yourself: what was the clear, sharp thing that has now lost its clarity? That will always point you to the exact meaning in context.
The most common phrases you'll encounter

Blurred lines is perhaps the most common — it means the separating line between two things is no longer clear. Blurred boundaries refers to roles, spaces, or categories that are not well-defined. Blurred vision is the everyday and medical term for eyesight that is fuzzy and out of focus. Blurred memories are recollections that are hazy and imprecise. A blurred image is simply a picture that is out of focus.

Something is blurred when it lacks sharpness, clarity, or clear definition — whether you are looking at it with your eyes, or trying to determine where one idea, category, role, or concept ends and another begins.
